source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / ASPIRE Project, IFAD-funded - "ដំណាំក្រូចថ្លុង" (Pomelo Cultivation Guide), 2017, 90pp
text:
Citrus leaf miner (ដង្កូវសិទ្ធកញ្ចង់, Phyllocnistis citrella, family Gracillariidae) is a small moth whose larvae tunnel just under the surface of young citrus leaves, leaving silvery, winding trails visible on the leaf. Heavily mined leaves curl, become distorted, and photosynthesize poorly, which is especially damaging to young trees and new flushes of growth that nurseries depend on for healthy development.

The adult moth is small and pale with silvery-white wings; it lays eggs on the underside of young, still-expanding leaves, and the newly hatched larva burrows directly into the leaf tissue to begin mining, pupating inside a fold at the leaf margin before emerging as an adult.

Control measures include monitoring new flushes closely (since only young, soft leaves are attacked), pruning and destroying heavily mined leaves and shoots to reduce the pest population, encouraging natural predators and parasitic wasps, and timing any insecticide application to new flush periods when larvae are still small and exposed, rather than spraying on a fixed schedule.
